allowfullscreen="true" width="728" height="409"></iframe></div></div><blockquote><p>“I would argue the biggest risk is actually locking in a very narrow monoculture for superintelligence. One superintelligence is much less safe than infinite superintelligence.” — Vincent Weisser</p></blockquote><div class="pullquote"><p><strong><span>Listen or watch now on</span><br><a href="https://youtu.be/gTi-VYAPbKY">YouTube</a><span>, </span><a href="https://open.spotify.com/episode/5bFsR8D5ppjZJ4C8LSX5Gf">Spotify</a><span>, or </span><a href="https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/why-one-superintelligence-is-more-dangerous-than-a/id1805868710?i=1000756982181">Apple Podcasts</a></strong></p></div><p><span>Much of the fear around AI centers on misalignment – the idea that powerful systems might act against human interests. </span><strong>Vincent Weisser</strong><span> worries about something different: what happens if advanced AI systems are perfectly aligned with the interests of a small group of institutions? That concern led him to co-found Prime Intellect, a startup building open infrastructure for training and deploying advanced AI models. Before Prime Intellect, Weisser helped organize Vitalik Buterin’s Zuzalu experiment and worked in decentralized science, where he helped unlock roughly $40 million in funding for unconventional research. Today, he’s applying that same open ethos to AI, working to ensure the tools that shape superintelligence remain broadly accessible rather than concentrated in the hands of a few.</span></p><p><strong>In our conversation, we explore:</strong></p><ul><li><p>Why Vincent believes multiple superintelligences are safer than one</p></li><li><p>The intellectual influences that shaped Vincent’s thinking about intelligence and progress, including David Deutsch and Nick Bostrom</p></li><li><p>Prime Intellect’s evolution from distributed compute infrastructure to frontier model training and reinforcement learning tools</p></li><li><p>Why Vincent believes open and decentralized science could accelerate discovery</p></li><li><p>The Zuzalu experiment and what it suggests about the future of scientific communities</p></li><li><p>The role of aesthetics and craft in building technology</p></li><li><p>Why Europe might have a cultural advantage in a post-superintelligence One superintelligence is much less safe than infinite superintelligence.\u201D \u2014 Vincent Weisser</p></blockquote><div class=\\\"pullquote\\\"><p><strong>Listen or watch now on<br><a href=\\\"https://youtu.be/gTi-VYAPbKY\\\">YouTube</a>, <a href=\\\"https://open.spotify.com/episode/5bFsR8D5ppjZJ4C8LSX5Gf\\\">Spotify</a>, or <a href=\\\"https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/why-one-superintelligence-is-more-dangerous-than-a/id1805868710?i=1000756982181\\\">Apple Podcasts</a></strong></p></div><p>Much of the fear around AI centers on misalignment \u2013 the idea that powerful systems might act against human interests. <strong>Vincent Weisser</strong> worries about something different: what happens if advanced AI systems are perfectly aligned with the interests of a small group of institutions? That concern led him to co-found Prime Intellect, a startup building open infrastructure for training and deploying advanced AI models. Before Prime Intellect, Weisser helped organize Vitalik Buterin\u2019s Zuzalu experiment and worked in decentralized science, where he helped unlock roughly $40 million in funding for unconventional research. Today, he\u2019s applying that same open ethos to AI, working to ensure the tools that shape superintelligence remain broadly accessible rather than concentrated in the hands of a few.</p><p><strong>In our conversation, we explore:</strong></p><ul><li><p>Why Vincent believes multiple superintelligences are safer than one</p></li><li><p>The intellectual influences that shaped Vincent\u2019s thinking about intelligence and progress, including David Deutsch and Nick Bostrom</p></li><li><p>Prime Intellect\u2019s evolution from distributed compute infrastructure to frontier model training and reinforcement learning tools</p></li><li><p>Why Vincent believes open and decentralized science could accelerate discovery</p></li><li><p>The Zuzalu experiment and what it suggests about the future of scientific communities</p></li><li><p>The role of aesthetics and craft in building technology</p></li><li><p>Why Europe might have a cultural advantage in a post-superintelligence
